lessons.title: Network Security and the TCP/IP Model

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following protocols operates at the Internet layer of the TCP/IP model?
A) HTTP
B) SMTP
C) TCP
D) IP
Name two protocols that operate at the Application layer of the TCP/IP model.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any two of: HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP, IMAP. [1 mark for two correct answers]

practice_questions.text: State one difference between a firewall and MAC address filtering as network security measures.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A firewall monitors and filters data packets based on rules about the content and source/destination of traffic; MAC address filtering controls which devices can connect to the network based on their hardware address, operating before data is transmitted.
Secure: Correct contrast identifying the different aspect each measure targets.
Developing: Describes one measure accurately, the other vaguely.
Emerging: Names both without meaningful comparison. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what encryption does to data and why it is important for network security.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Encryption converts data into ciphertext using a key so it cannot be read by anyone who intercepts it in transit. Only the holder of the correct decryption key can restore it. This is critical for protecting sensitive data such as passwords, financial details and messages on a network, even if an attacker gains access to the data stream.
Secure: Correct explanation of encryption with a clear security benefit.
Developing: States data is scrambled/unreadable but does not explain the key mechanism or security benefit clearly.
Emerging: Vague description — e.g. 'makes data safe' without explanation. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of each of the four layers of the TCP/IP model. Name at least one protocol or hardware component associated with each layer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All four layers accurately described with correct protocols/hardware: Application (HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP, IMAP — where applications operate), Transport (TCP — sets up communication, manages packets, ensures delivery), Internet (IP — addressing and routing packets), Link (NIC, OS drivers — physical transmission). Explains the flow of data down through layers on send and up on receive.
Secure: All four layers identified with accurate roles; some protocols/hardware correctly placed.
Developing: Three layers described with mostly correct protocols; one layer confused or missing.
Emerging: Two or fewer layers described; protocols placed at incorrect layers. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: A school wants to prevent unauthorised devices from connecting to its wireless network. Explain how MAC address filtering works and identify one limitation of this approach.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Every NIC has a unique MAC address assigned by its manufacturer. The network administrator creates a list of approved MAC addresses; only devices on the list are permitted to connect, even if they know the Wi-Fi password. Limitation: MAC addresses can be changed in software (MAC spoofing), allowing an attacker to impersonate an approved device.
Secure: Correct explanation of how filtering works and a valid limitation.
Developing: Explains that only approved devices can connect but does not explain how the filtering is applied; or explains correctly without identifying a limitation.
Emerging: Vague description of blocking devices. [4 marks]

lessons.title: Cyber Security Threats and Social Engineering

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes pharming?
A) Sending fraudulent emails to trick users into revealing their passwords
B) Physically watching someone enter a PIN at a cashpoint
C) Redirecting users from a legitimate website to a fraudulent one without them clicking a malicious link
D) Using a fabricated scenario to trick someone into revealing information over the phone
practice_questions.marks: C) Redirecting users from a legitimate website to a fraudulent one without them clicking a malicious link [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two types of malware that are covered in this topic.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any two of: computer virus / trojan / spyware. [1 mark for two correct answers]

practice_questions.text: State the difference between blagging and phishing as forms of social engineering.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Blagging involves creating a fabricated scenario (pretext) — typically in a phone call or face-to-face interaction — to manipulate someone into revealing information. Phishing uses fraudulent emails or messages to trick users into visiting a fake site or providing credentials.
Secure: Correct distinction between the medium/method of each.
Developing: Vague distinction — e.g. one involves emails, the other phone calls — without explaining the mechanism.
Emerging: Names both without meaningful comparison. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a computer virus spreads and describe one way an organisation could protect itself from virus infections.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A virus attaches itself to a legitimate file; when the file is opened or shared (e.g. as an email attachment or via a USB drive), the virus copies itself to other files or systems. Protection: keeping anti-malware software up to date so it detects known virus signatures; or disabling autorun on removable media to prevent viruses spreading automatically.
Secure: Spread correctly explained; protection method valid and linked to the mechanism.
Developing: Spread described vaguely or protection described without link to virus behaviour.
Emerging: Identifies viruses as harmful without explaining spread. [2 marks per part]

practice_questions.text: Explain what penetration testing is and describe the difference between internal and external penetration testing.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Penetration testing is the authorised process of attempting to access a system without normal credentials to find and fix vulnerabilities. Internal testing: the tester has some knowledge or credentials, simulating a malicious insider. External testing: the tester has no knowledge or credentials, simulating an outside attacker. Both types aim to identify weaknesses before real attackers exploit them.
Secure: Correct definition and both types distinguished with the key credential/knowledge difference.
Developing: Correct definition; types partially distinguished.
Emerging: Describes penetration testing vaguely; does not distinguish between types. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A company discovers that many staff are using weak passwords and running unpatched software. Explain why each of these poses a security risk and suggest one measure for each to reduce the risk.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Weak passwords — easily guessed or cracked by automated tools; risk is unauthorised access. Measure: enforce a password policy (minimum length, mixed characters) or use multi-factor authentication. Unpatched software — known vulnerabilities are publicly documented; attackers write exploits targeting them. Measure: configure automatic updates or establish a regular patching schedule. Both risks connected to real consequences (data breach, service disruption). Measures evaluated for effectiveness.
Secure: Both risks accurately explained with appropriate measures.
Developing: Both risks identified; measures partially correct or not linked to the specific risk.
Emerging: One risk explained; measure vague or missing. [8 marks]
